difference.question: How is DramaClaw different from an ordinary AI video generator?
difference.answer: Ordinary tools work around a single prompt, a single clip, or a single image. DramaClaw is built around a complete project: text import, asset build-up, episode planning, shot production and final compositing — a traceable, collaborative, reusable production loop.

gettingStarted.question: Where should I start the first time?
gettingStarted.answer: Follow the main workflow: import your text in Shrimp Feed, confirm characters / scenes / props / voices in Shrimp Pond, plan episodes and generate scripts and shots in Shrimp Lens, then export the cut from the compositing page. The first goal isn't perfection — it's getting one episode all the way through.

mirrorVsCanvas.question: What are Shrimp Lens and Shrimp Canvas each good for?
mirrorVsCanvas.answer: Shrimp Lens is the main production line: batch work, stability, episode-by-episode progress. Shrimp Canvas is the director's workbench: polishing key shots, exploring versions, finalising assets and heavier video work. On a real project, ordinary shots run through Shrimp Lens and the hard ones go to Shrimp Canvas.

canvasOverwrite.question: Do results in Shrimp Canvas overwrite my mainline assets automatically?
canvasOverwrite.answer: No. Anything generated or uploaded in Shrimp Canvas is a candidate by default. It only enters the project mainline once you explicitly commit it and pick a target slot — character, scene, prop, beat sketch, first frame or video.

whyAssetsFirst.question: Why organise characters, scenes, props and voices first?
whyAssetsFirst.answer: The usual cause of rework in AI video isn't the final generation step — it's unstable characters, vague scenes, props without references and inconsistent voices upstream. Turning those into assets in Shrimp Pond removes a lot of chaos from the shot stage.

contentTypes.question: What kinds of content is DramaClaw suited to?
contentTypes.answer: AI short dramas, comic dramas, novel promos, commentary shows, ads, and training videos — plus team projects that maintain IP characters and serialised content over time. Solo creators can run the whole pipeline; teams can produce collaboratively.

teamRoles.question: How should a team divide the work?
teamRoles.answer: Split it by stage: the owner manages the project, cost and QA; the writer handles text and scripts; the art lead maintains characters, scenes and props; the storyboard/director owns shot performance; the video operator handles first frames, video and compositing. Permissions map to viewer, editor, admin and owner.

unstableResults.question: What should I check first when results are inconsistent?
unstableResults.answer: Find the stage that's failing: is the text clear, is the character identity right, do the scene and props have references, does the sketch describe the shot, is the first frame stable, does the audio match? Don't start by regenerating video over and over — fix the upstream assets and the shot description first.

dcUniverse.question: What does “Make Your DC Universe.” mean?
dcUniverse.answer: DC isn't only short for DramaClaw — it also stands for each creator's own content universe. DramaClaw is meant to help you start from one story and build up characters, world, scene assets and the ability to produce a series.

afterLogin.question: Where do I land after logging in?
afterLogin.answer: In the project hub. You can open an existing project or create a new one to start a new series. Each project is its own space, holding text, assets, episodes, shots, video, tasks and composited results.

macGatekeeper.question: macOS says the developer cannot be verified. Now what?
macGatekeeper.answer: Find DramaClaw in Finder → Applications, Control-click the icon, choose Open, then confirm with Open in the dialog. You only do this once; after that it launches normally.

winSmartScreen.question: Windows says it protected my PC. Now what?
winSmartScreen.answer: Click More info, then Run anyway. SmartScreen blocks installers by default until they have enough downloads; it says nothing about whether this one is intact.

offline.question: Does the app still need an internet connection?
offline.answer: Yes. Script generation, first-frame rendering and video assembly all run on cloud compute; the app handles orchestration, media management and writing results to disk. Cuts already downloaded stay playable offline.

update.question: How do I upgrade?

storage.question: Where do projects and exports live?
storage.answer: Project data lives in the cloud with your account, so every device signed in sees the same episodes. Exported boards, first frames and finished cuts are written to local disk, and you can change that path in settings.

novelFormat.title: Premium drama format
novelFormat.intro: Premium drama scripts need explicit episode and scene boundaries. DramaClaw splits the script by scene headers before generating visuals, dialogue, and audio line by line; it does not invent scene breaks for headerless prose.
novelFormat.standardStatusHint: Several industry formats are supported. Complete location, time, and INT/EXT metadata can be parsed reliably.
novelFormat.warningStatusHint: Scene boundaries are clear, but location, time, or INT/EXT metadata is incomplete and will be normalized.
novelFormat.blockingStatusHint: Import is blocked only when chapters are invalid or a premium drama has no recognizable scene headings.
novelFormat.repairableHint: Both scenes below are understood, but each is missing something: “SCENE 1 - TITLE” has no time or INT/EXT, and “INT./EXT.” cannot be resolved to a single interior/exterior value. Either one downgrades the whole script to “repairable” — import is allowed with a warning and the gaps are filled in later. The source text is never rewritten.
novelFormat.ruleEpisode: Start every episode with “EPISODE 1” on its own line; list multiple episodes in order. “CHAPTER 1” is accepted as well.
novelFormat.ruleScene: Give every scene a complete heading of its own: INT./EXT. + location + “ - ” + time, e.g. “INT. SEOUL SUBWAY STATION - NIGHT”. Do not fill the heading in only for the first scene of an episode.
novelFormat.ruleCharacters: List the characters physically present in the scene on a “Characters:” line right under the heading, separated by commas; keep identity and performance notes out of that line.
novelFormat.ruleBody: Write action on “△ ” lines, one visible shot per line (“▲” works too). Do not pack several shots or speakers onto one line.
novelFormat.ruleDialogue: Write dialogue as “JI-WON: Is anyone here?” — a bare uppercase character name on its own line is not recognized as a speaker. Add a short cue in parentheses only when needed, and use “JI-WON OS: …” for inner voice.
novelFormat.ruleLocationChange: Open a new scene heading whenever the physical location changes. Use INT. for interior and EXT. for exterior — a complete heading needs one of the two.
novelFormat.ruleTimeTokens: Only DAY, NIGHT, MORNING, AFTERNOON, EVENING, DAWN and DUSK are accepted in the time slot. Anything else (MIDNIGHT, LATE NIGHT, a bare clock time) makes the whole heading unrecognizable, so the scene boundary is lost.
novelFormat.ruleClockTime: Never put a clock time inside the location name. When you need one, add a separate “Time: 11:47 PM” line under the heading — the location stays “Seoul Subway Station” and the time normalizes to night.

sceneHeaderMissingSlots.fix: Fill in the missing values from the actual scene — for example “{{suggestion}}”.

missingSceneHeaders.message: No scene headings were recognized, so the system cannot tell where each scene begins.
missingSceneHeaders.fix: Follow the standard format: start every episode with “Episode N”, give each scene its own “scene number, location, time, INT/EXT” heading, then list characters, action, and dialogue. For example: Episode 1 / 1-1 City Cafe DAY INT.

nonstandardSceneHeaders.message: Scene boundaries were recognized, but some scene metadata is incomplete.
nonstandardSceneHeaders.fix: The system recognized the scene boundaries and will complete or normalize the missing location, time, and INT/EXT values during scene planning.

sceneHeadersMissingTime.message: Some scene headings have no explicit time anchor, so time_of_day and scene variant inheritance may be unstable.
sceneHeadersMissingTime.fix: Add an explicit time to the scene heading, such as DAY, NIGHT, or LATE NIGHT. Scene boundaries are kept either way and normalized later.

missingInteriorExterior.message: The scene heading has no INT/EXT marker.
missingInteriorExterior.fix: Add INT or EXT, as in “location time INT/EXT”.

sparseSceneHeaders.message: There are few scene headings, so continuous scenes and time inheritance may be unstable.
sparseSceneHeaders.fix: Add one scene heading per scene.

tooFewDialogueLines.message: Few usable dialogue lines were found. If this is a silent or action-driven passage, you can still import it.
tooFewDialogueLines.fix: Add recognizable dialogue lines in the form “Character: line”.

multiSpeakerLines.message: Several lines pack multiple speakers or colons onto one line. The system will try to normalize them as a B-grade script, but one line per spoken line is better.
multiSpeakerLines.fix: Rewrite so each line holds a single spoken line from a single speaker.

ambiguousSpeakers.message: Many speakers are ambiguous (“he”, “she”, “the other party”, “the voice on the phone”), so identity resolution may be unstable.
ambiguousSpeakers.fix: Replace vague speakers such as “he” or “she” with the actual character names.

manyLongDialogues.message: There are many very long single dialogue lines, which tend to produce over-long single-unit dialogue later.
manyLongDialogues.fix: Split the longest lines to reduce the length of a single dialogue line.

duplicateChapterNumber.fix: Check for sentences in the body that look like chapter titles, so one chapter number is not split into several chapters.

nonIncreasingChapterNumber.message: The chapter number goes from {{previous_number}} back to or repeats {{number}}.
nonIncreasingChapterNumber.fix: Check that chapter numbers increase, or confirm that chapter-like wording in the body was not mistaken for a title.

notScreenplayLike.message: The text reads more like novel prose than a scene-based script. This check does not block the import, but the structured result may be weaker.
notScreenplayLike.fix: If this is novel prose, switch the project type to Narrated. If it is a script, add the scene headings.
